hints: Look closely at what happens to the starting haloalkane, is something adding across a double bond or is one group swapping for another?
Remember that $\text{NH}_3$ has a lone pair on nitrogen, so think about what kind of reagent it acts as when it attacks the $\delta+$ carbon in $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{I}$.
Put those two ideas together, a lone-pair donor replacing iodide, to decide between addition and substitution and between nucleophilic and electrophilic.
walkthrough:
**Spot the pattern in the equation**

Look at the change from reactant to product. The $\text{I}$ in iodoethane is swapped for $\text{NH}_2$.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{I} + 2\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{NH}_4\text{I}$$

**Decide substitution or addition**

There is no $\text{C=C}$ double bond here, so nothing can add across it. One group leaves and another takes its place, so this must be substitution.

**Decide nucleophilic or electrophilic**

Nitrogen in $\text{NH}_3$ has a lone pair, so it is a nucleophile (a lone-pair donor). It attacks the electron-deficient $\delta+$ carbon attached to iodine.

$$\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{I}^{\delta-} + :\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}-\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{I}^-$$

**Name the mechanism**

A nucleophile doing a replacement gives nucleophilic substitution. The second $\text{NH}_3$ simply removes a proton to give the free amine and $\text{NH}_4\text{I}$.

options.A: Electrophilic addition happens to alkenes when an electrophile attacks the pi bond. Here we have a saturated haloalkane with no double bond, and the attacker is a nucleophile, not an electrophile.
options.B: Free-radical substitution needs radicals, usually made by UV light, as in alkane with halogen. This reaction uses ammonia with its lone pair in the dark, with no radicals involved.
options.C: Nucleophilic addition happens to polar double bonds like C=O in aldehydes and ketones. Here there is no double bond to add to, an atom is replaced instead, so it is substitution.
options.D: This is correct. Ammonia acts as a nucleophile and replaces iodide on the haloalkane. That is the classic nucleophilic substitution route from halogenoalkane to amine.
